newsitem.title: USA: Democrats eye second Oregon Senate seat in a year.
newsitem.headline: Democrats eye second Oregon Senate seat in a year.

text.p: Republican Gordon Smith, a frozen-food mogul, hopes to have more luck this time round as he mounts his second campaign this year for a Senate seat.

But Democrat Tom Bruggere, a self-made computer-software millionaire, believes he can block Smith and complete a Democratic takeover of Oregon's two Senate seats, which until this year had been in Republican hands for 28 years.

Smith, president of family-owned Smith's Frozen Foods, and Bruggere, founder and former chief executive officer of Mentor Graphics Corp., are locked in a close and increasingly bitter race to succeed Republican Sen. Mark Hatfield, who is retiring after 30 years.
A poll late last month showed the two candidates nearly even -- with Bruggere leading Smith 44 percent to 40 -- within the survey's margin of error.

The race has drawn considerable interest from the national tickets of both parties. President Clinton and Vice President Gore, strongly favoured to take Oregon, campaigned in the state last month after a bus tour and helped Bruggere raise funds.
Republican candidate Bob Dole stumped in the state for Smith and his running mate Jack Kemp was in Portland on Friday for a rally.

The race was Smith's second Senate campaign in a year. He was narrowly defeated by Democrat Ron Wyden in a January special election to replace Republican Sen. Bob Packwood, who resigned in a sexual harassment scandal.
Smith spent more than $2 million of his own money in the race with Wyden and was ready to swear off politics when it was over.

"I was devastated," he told Reuters. "But one of the first phone calls I got after the election was from Mark Hatfield. He told me to dust myself off, get up and keep running and he would help me win."
Both Smith and Bruggere are relative newcomers to politics.
Smith served one term in the state Senate but was elected Senate president in the second half of that term.
Bruggere served as an adviser on education to Democratic Govs. Neil Goldschmidt and John Kitzhaber.
"I am not a politician," Bruggere told Reuters. "I have never run for anything before. I am very independent and not simply a party loyalist."
Bruggere also likes to stress that his is something of a Horatio Alger story.

He grew up in Oregon, the son of a travelling candy salesman, attended public school and worked his way through college pumping gasoline for minimum wage. He enlisted and fought as an infantryman in Vietnam and attended graduate school on the GI bill, studying computer science.

Bruggere and some friends founded Mentor Graphics in his living room in the early 1980s. He retired in 1994, but not before he built a company headquarters surrounded by wetlands and created a reputation as an environmentalist.

Smith, by contrast, grew up in Washington, D.C., the son of a former deputy secretary of agriculture. After attending law school, he moved to Oregon in 1980 to take over a troubled food processing plant owned by his family in Pendleton.
He modernised the plant, turned the business around and made himself wealthy. The plant employs about 1,000 people.
Both men dipped into their personal fortunes, estimated at $20 million each, to finance their campaigns. Bruggere spent $1 million on his primary campaign.
Smith, 43, favours Dole's proposed 15 percent tax cut and wants to see less government interference in people's lives.
"My opponent is someone who believes that government has all the answers." Smith said. "I believe government is big enough."
Bruggere, 50, countered that Smith favoured giving tax breaks to the wealthy, gutting the nation's environmental laws and weakening the education system.

He charged that Smith's food plant has "one of the worst environmental records in the state." The plant was fined for violating clean water standards by making discharges into a stream but recently had all its wastewater permits renewed.

Smith also accused Bruggere in ads and speeches of launching a background investigation of his wife and deceased father in an effort to dig up dirt for a negative campaign. Bruggere denied the accusation and countered with a television ad depicting Smith as a small child who likes to "sling mud."
